1:
Which Herod this was has to be settled first, and the answers converge. Barnes and Wesley both identify him as Agrippa, grandson of Herod the Great and son of the Aristobulus whom his own father put to death; Robertson dates the reign exactly, Herod Agrippa the First being king of Palestine for three years only, since after the death of Herod the Great no Herod was king again, and calls the title in the text accurate at this particular moment. Ellicott fills in the career that made such a man possible: sent to Rome as a boy after his father fell victim to his grandfather's suspicions, partly as a hostage and partly to be out of the way of Palestine intrigues, growing up intimate with the prince who became Caligula, made ruler of Tiberias, quarrelling with the Tetrarch, falling under the displeasure of Tiberius. Calvin is interested in the timing rather than the man, noting that the church had enjoyed a short truce and warning the faithful not to expect perpetual rest after one or two conflicts, as worn-out soldiers expect a discharge, but to be content if the Lord grants time to recover strength.

On the death of James the manner of execution is read as evidence. Ellicott argues that had the apostle been tried by the Sanhedrin for blasphemy the sentence would have been stoning, so that decapitation shows a civil ruler pronouncing sentence and adopting Roman punishments, terrifying the Jews in proportion as those punishments were hateful to them. Lightfoot supplies the Jewish side of the same point from the rabbinic sources, where four kinds of death are said to be delivered into the hands of the Sanhedrim, killing with the sword among them. Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley all notice the same fulfilment, that the sons of Zebedee had asked to sit at the right hand and left, and were told they should drink of their Lord's cup; Wesley puts it most compactly, that one brother went to God first of the apostles and the other last. Clarke adds a consequence the others pass over, that by this death the number of the apostles was reduced to eleven and was never filled up, since the apostles had no successors. Robertson admits an unanswered question, why Luke says so little of this death and so much of Stephen's.

The motive is agreed to be popularity and not zeal. Calvin observes that persecution has more than one cause, since a perverse zeal sometimes drives men to shed innocent blood for their superstitions while the greater part are moved only by private advantage, and Herod belongs to the second sort. Gill and Barnes say the same, Barnes adding the political pressure behind it, that a ruler holding his appointment from Rome needed the goodwill of a people to whom foreign rule was always unpopular. Ellicott illustrates the king's sensitivity with a story: hearing the law read at the Feast of Tabernacles, at the words about not setting a stranger over thee, he burst into tears at the thought of his own Idumaean descent, until the people cried out that he too was their brother. On the custody Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree on the arithmetic, four companies of four making sixteen men, relieved by watches, the prisoner chained to two while two more kept the door. Clarke reserves his indignation for the translators, calling the rendering of the festival as Easter perhaps the most unhappy ever made, and Ellicott agrees the word belongs only to the Christian feast.
6:
The sleeping prisoner is the detail all of them stop on. Barnes calls it an instance of remarkable composure and a proof of peace of conscience, since Peter knew what Herod intended and had just seen James put to death, and yet slept. Ellicott finds in it one to whom God had given the sleep of his beloved, and Henry a peaceful conscience with a lively hope keeping a man calm in the full prospect of death, even a man once distracted with terrors on that account. Wesley says it in five words, easy and void of fear. Robertson and Clarke both explain the arrangement that made the composure remarkable, one chain fastened to each of two soldiers lying on either side of him while two more kept the door, and Robertson wonders whether Peter recalled the word of Jesus that he should be put to death in his old age. Calvin turns to the prayers of the church and answers the objection that they seemed to be too late: God often takes his time at the last and farthest point of necessity, and they may have prayed less for Peter's life than that he might be armed with invincible fortitude.

Barnes considers whether the light was lightning and rejects the notion, since light and splendour commonly accompany heavenly visitors, and he thinks it was seen by Peter alone and served him as proof of divine interposition. Calvin reasons the same way about who saw it, supposing the soldiers slept too soundly or were too amazed to perceive anything, and offers two possible purposes, that Peter might have the use of the light in the darkness or that it might be a token to him of the heavenly glory. Ellicott notes that the phrase is word for word the one used of the shepherds at the nativity, and that the Greek article leaves it open whether to read the angel or an angel. Robertson observes that the verb for the angel's sudden standing by is a form Luke uses seven times in his Gospel and eight in the Acts and no other writer uses at all, and that the matching form for the angel's departure appears a few verses later. Barnes and Clarke agree the blow on the side was gentle, just enough to wake him, and Ellicott adds that the word rendered prison here means properly a dwelling or chamber, used as a euphemism.

On the wards Clarke supposes three walls about the old city and successive gates through them, the prison standing at the outer one and the iron gate at the inner, plated over for security as eastern gates still are; Ellicott reads the movement the other way, from the innermost dungeon outward across two courtyards, and reports that Lightfoot put the prison between the inner and outer walls. Robertson admits the language is not clear and canvasses whether the wards mean single soldiers or further guards beyond the sixteen, but observes that on any reading the difficulties of escape are made plain. Calvin asks why the deliverance was staged at all, since God could have carried Peter away in a moment, and answers that he overcomes one strait after another so that the glory of the miracle might be greater, as he made the world in six days not from need of time but to hold us in the meditation of his works. Clarke has no patience with a rationalising divine who made the angel an illusion and credited the escape to a friendly prefect, and Robertson notes that Peter was still in peril until the guard changed at six.
12:
The house belonged to a woman, and the commentators build on that. Ellicott gathers five inferences about the family: that Mark was probably converted by Peter, who calls him his son; that he was cousin to Barnabas and therefore at least connected with the tribe of Levi; that Mary's house serving as the meeting place indicates comparative wealth; that the absence of any mention of a father makes it likely she was a widow; and that the identification of this Mark with the evangelist is probable. Calvin infers her rare godliness from the same fact, her house being as it were a certain temple of God, and reasons that the brethren must have met in companies at several places in the city, since one house could not hold them all and a single gathering could not avoid the fear of tumult. Robertson notes that Peter's mind worked rapidly and the verb used is the one from which the word for conscience comes, a seeing of the whole situation at once. Henry draws the practical rule, that God's providence leaves room for the use of our prudence even where he has undertaken to finish what he began.

Rhoda gets more attention than her few words might warrant. Ellicott takes the mention of a slave's name as evidence of Luke's care in ascertaining details so far as his opportunities allowed, and notes that opening the door to strangers was commonly a female slave's office, as it was even at the high priest's palace. Barnes and Clarke both explain the name, which means a rose, and both borrow from Grotius the observation that Hebrews gave their daughters the names of flowers and trees, instancing Susanna a lily, Hadassah a myrtle and Tamar a palm. Ellicott extends the same list with a bee and a pearl and an antelope. Robertson distinguishes the two words used for the entrance, one the door itself and the other the passageway leading from it to the house, and glosses her coming to hearken as listening under the door before opening it. Clarke supposes the door was shut for fear of the Jews and that Peter stood knocking at an outer gate across the courtyard, which is why she had to go and listen at all.

That the praying church disbelieved the answer is not passed over. Barnes states the irony plainly, that the very thing they had been earnestly asking was announced and they called the messenger insane, which shows with how little faith men often pray and how slow they are to believe that what they sought could be granted. Gill offers a defence, that they may have been praying in faith without expecting deliverance, asking rather that Peter might be supported and kept faithful to the last and bear a glorious testimony by his death. Henry says that what we most earnestly wish for we are often most backward to believe. On the guardian angel Clarke and Ellicott both report the Jewish belief that every man has one which assumes his likeness when it appears, Clarke adding the stories of Elijah appearing in the likeness of various rabbins, and Ellicott cautioning that the record of a casual utterance of such a belief cannot be taken as authoritative sanction of it. Clarke notes besides that the word may simply mean a messenger sent from Peter. On the closing charge Clarke observes that Peter defers to James and finds in that no supremacy for Peter.
18:
Chrysostom raises the question the narrative leaves open, why God should look on quietly while the soldiers are put to death for Peter's escape, when it was possible to have rescued them too. He answers that it was not yet the time of judgment, when each is rendered his deserts, and adds that it was not Peter who put them into Herod's hands; what most annoyed the king was being mocked, as his grandfather had been cut to the heart by the wise men, the being made ridiculous. He notices too that Herod had heard from the soldiers under examination that the chains were left behind and that the prisoner had taken his sandals. Robertson describes the scene from the soldiers' side, since all sixteen would have been agitated by so remarkable an escape and were answerable for the prisoner with their lives; and he reports a suggestion that the king's Christian foster-brother was the angel who freed Peter, remarking only that this is not how Peter looked at it. Barnes states the same exposure plainly, that the punishment they had reason to expect for allowing an escape was death.

Calvin reads the examination as a judicial proceeding that convicted the judge. Herod could not suspect that Peter was taken by violence or escaped by some subtle shift, so that when he perceived the soldiers were in no fault he was himself compelled to be a witness of a deliverance wrought by God; and Calvin calls it an excellent example of blindness that a man should see so much and be moved so little. He hesitates over what the command actually was, since the words may mean either that the men were carried off to prison or that they were dragged immediately to execution, and he allows both readings, tracing the first to rage mixed with tyrannous cruelty and shame. Ellicott settles the phrase as half-technical and half-euphemistic, literally that they should be led away, and notes that capital punishment was by Roman usage the almost inevitable penalty for letting a prisoner escape, which is why the gaoler at Philippi was on the point of anticipating sentence by suicide. Robertson agrees this was ordinary Roman routine and no proof of special cruelty in Herod, and Clarke says the keepers ordinarily suffered what the prisoner would have suffered.

Barnes observes what Herod plainly did not admit, since a rigid scrutiny of the guards shows the king had no intention of allowing the possibility of a miraculous interposition, and he notes that no further inquiry after Peter is recorded. On the removal to Caesarea, Barnes says the place was rising into magnificence and the Roman governors often made it their residence, and reports that Josephus dates the journey after three years of reign over all Judea; Robertson adds the particular occasion, that Herod Agrippa kept his home at Jerusalem and went down for the public games in honour of the emperor. Clarke and Barnes both confess they do not know how soon he went or how long he stayed. Robertson notes the idiom in which the question about Peter is put, an indirect construction asking literally what Peter had become, and the figure by which no small stir means a very great one, a turn of speech Luke uses eight times in this book and no other writer uses at all. Barnes reads the verse as ending the episode, since Herod abode there until his death, which followed shortly.
20:
Why Herod quarrelled with the Phoenician cities nobody knows, and Clarke says so, noting that Josephus, who records the journey, passes the matter over and that conjecture is useless. Barnes and Robertson both guess at commerce all the same, Barnes supposing the cities may have embarrassed the king's regulations, Robertson observing that Phoenicia belonged to Syria and Herod had no authority there, so that the quarrel may have been over trade. Ellicott explains what made the cities anxious, that with large populations on narrow strips of territory they depended on imported corn and oil and wine, and that the same commercial relation appears in the days of Solomon and again in Ezekiel. Lightfoot brings the second of those passages forward for the same purpose. Wesley draws out a consequence the others leave implicit, that the reconciliation delivered the Christians of those parts from scarcity by the providence of God. On the approach through the chamberlain, Clarke supposes Blastus a eunuch with considerable influence over his master, so that reaching the king meant bribing the servant; Robertson notes that Josephus, who tells the whole story, does not mention his name.

The parallel in Josephus is set beside the text by nearly everyone, and the agreement is what interests them. Barnes quotes the historian at length, that when Agrippa had reigned three years over all Judea he came to Caesarea and exhibited shows in honour of Caesar. Clarke and Wesley both give the detail of the robe, a garment wrought wholly of silver whose contexture was truly wonderful, worn into the theatre early in the morning so that the first rays of the sun struck it and it shone out resplendent. Ellicott adds that such a robe was what Caligula had worn at banquets in Rome, and that the courtiers were taking up a Roman fashion of honouring emperors when they hailed the king as a god. Robertson dates the occasion to the second day of a festival for Claudius, possibly his birthday, and judges that the two accounts supplement each other with no contradiction. Calvin makes the same comparison more carefully still, noting that Josephus calls him Agrippa throughout where Luke calls him Herod, and suggesting that Agrippa was his own name while the other was the dynastic title he assumed on becoming king.

Barnes is careful about what the stroke was and was not. Diseases and death are often ascribed to an angel in the Scriptures, so a miracle need not be intended, though the sacred writer certainly means the death for a divine judgment on a man who accepted homage as a god; and he quotes Josephus, who says the king neither rebuked the people nor rejected their impious flattery before a severe pain arose in his belly and wore him out over five days. Lightfoot notes that the historian speaks more sparingly than Luke, mentioning only the pains that came thick upon him. Henry makes the pride the whole point, since the measure of Herod's iniquity was filled up by it, and observes that God reckoned with him not merely for putting James to death but for the endeavour against Peter, sinners being answerable for the mischief they would have done as well as for what they did. Calvin reads the episode as a glass showing both the end prepared for the enemies of the church and how greatly God hates pride, and turns it on the reader: if pride was punished so sharply in a king, what shall become of common men.
24:
Clarke hears agricultural language in the summary and works it out: the two verbs describe corn growing into stalk and ear and then being multiplied in the full ear, so that the sentence probably alludes to the parable of the sower, where the seed is the word of God. He adds his own account of why it grew, that there was no corruption in it and that God watered it from on high. Ellicott takes the tense as describing a continuous expansion and gives the plain historical cause, that the death of the chief persecutor left free scope for the preachers. Robertson calls it the reaction from the death of James and the imprisonment of Peter. Barnes gathers several effects at once, that the liberation and the death together were a new evidence of divine interposition which would augment the zeal of Christians, humble their enemies, and fill with fear those who had attempted to crush the church. Calvin puts it as a general rule with a figure to carry it, that when the tyrant was taken away the church was delivered as out of the jaws of the wolf, and that though the faithful are counted sheep for the slaughter the church always outlives her enemies.

On the return there is a textual difficulty and Robertson meets it head on. The likely reading is that Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem, though two of the great uncials give to Jerusalem, which he calls an impossible reading contradicted by what stands on either side of it in the narrative; and he notes that the aorist participle for taking Mark along does not express action later than the main verb, against a commentator who had argued so. Gill reports that several witnesses and the Syriac supply the destination, unto Antioch, which is certainly right since that is where they were sent from and where the next chapter finds them. Barnes and Calvin both identify the ministry that was fulfilled as the carrying of alms, gathered at Antioch after the prophet Agabus foretold the famine and entrusted to these two for the relief of the church at Jerusalem. Ellicott notes that the word used for it is the same one rendered relief when the collection was first described.

The man taken along interests them for what came of him. Ellicott explains the choice partly by his relationship to Barnabas but also as evidence that he entered heartily into the work among the Gentiles, and thinks that since he owed his conversion to Peter his going would naturally be read as a proof of that apostle's interest in the mission. Wesley and Clarke both identify him as the son of the Mary at whose house the disciples had met to pray for Peter, Clarke tracing his course from here to Cyprus and on until he left the apostles at Perga. Calvin sees the shadow already, noting that the man whose mother had just been honourably commended would afterwards be the cause of grievous and dangerous discord between the two who now took him. Barnes closes on the shape of the book rather than the men, observing that from this point the historian records chiefly the labours of Paul while the other apostles are seldom mentioned again, and suggesting that the reason may lie in the importance of those labours and in Luke having been his companion.
